title: Build a summary table with SUMIF
summary: Build a category summary table from one SUMIF formula with absolute references, then prove it with a grand-total cross-check.

blocks.text: Managers read summaries, not lists. A category summary shows sales per category in a few lines. The skill is writing one SUMIF formula that you copy down the whole table.

A summary can hide mistakes: a category spelt differently in the list falls out of every row of the table and the total quietly shrinks. A cross-check against the total of the original list catches that.

items: Objective: build a category summary with one copied SUMIF formula and a cross-check.
You pass the mission at 75% or more in the Assessment.

blocks.text: $A$2:$A$7 and $B$2:$B$7 have $ signs (absolute), so they stay put when the formula is copied down. E2 has no $ signs (relative), so it moves to E3, E4 and so on, picking up the next category.
Suppose the summary table lists Sneakers, Sandals and Boots in E2:E4, with their totals in F2:F4. Add them in F5 with SUM to get the total of the table.
The cross-check: compare the table total (cell F5 here) with the total of the original list. If they differ, some lines were not caught by any category, for example because of a spelling mistake.

items: Write the first formula, check it, then copy it down. Do not retype it on every row.
Absolute ($B$2:$B$7) for the list, relative (E2) for the label that changes.
A cross-check turns a hidden error into a visible message.
If the check says there is a problem, look for a category spelt differently in the list (for example Boot instead of Boots) or a category missing from the table.

blocks.text: Use the sales list from Training (A1:B7). Type whole numbers, for example 115.

items: Write one SUMIF with absolute ranges and a relative label, then copy it down.
Add the table with SUM to get a table total.
Compare the table total with SUM of the original list to catch missed lines.
Spelling differences (Boot versus Boots) are a common reason for a mismatch.

blocks.text: A summary with a built-in check is one you can trust and send to your manager.

items.prompt: Suppose row 7 had been typed as "Boot" instead of "Boots" (its sales are 110K). By how many K would the summary table total be below the total of the whole list?
In =SUMIF($A$2:$A$7,E2,$B$2:$B$7), which part is meant to change when the formula is copied down?

options.label: All three, so every row is different

items.prompt: What problem does the cross-check (table total versus list total) protect against?

options.label: Lines whose category does not match any row of the table, which would silently shrink the total
Rounding differences in the sales figures
Wrong prices in the price list
